extracted.intended_audience: aspiring poets, creative writers, and literary students/readers of criticism
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and evaluative criteria for writing and critiquing poetry, prose, drama, and characterisation, with emphasis on versification, diction, and moral/psychological plausibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Attention to metre and rhythm
rubrics_metrics.description: ‘His attention to metre and rhythm is sometimes so extremely minute as to be painful even to my ear, and you know how highly I prize good versification.’
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Value careful metrical and rhythmic control in poetry; examples include Coleridge's musical recitation of Spenser's Prothalamion with 'sensible diversity of tone and rhythm.' Anti-pattern: over-fastidiousness about metrical minutiae can become painful to the reader/listener.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prose vs. poetry—definition of distinction
rubrics_metrics.description: ‘Prose = words in their best order;--poetry = the best words in the best order.’
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this simple test when composing or judging: prose aims at good ordering of words; poetry demands selection of the best possible words as well as their ordering. Remind young poets of this homely definition as a compositional principle.

rubrics_metrics.name: Precise epithet and diction selection
rubrics_metrics.description: Anecdote: the author could not find a word for his feelings at the Falls of the Clyde until a stranger said 'How majestic!' and later 'how very pretty!'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose exact, appropriate epithets—avoid careless or conventional adjectival use (anti-pattern: applying epithets as boys do in making Latin verses). Strive for words that precisely capture the felt quality of a scene or object.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid cant; use common language
rubrics_metrics.description: Critique of religious writers: many adopt a certain cant of manner and phraseology as a token to each other; 'Why not use common language?'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer plain, common language over ritualized or fashionable jargon when sincerity and clarity are the aims. Anti-pattern: relying on stock cant ('in a prayerful way', 'the marrow of all religion') which obscures meaning and alienates readers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Character motivation must fit prior disposition
rubrics_metrics.description: On Othello: 'I have often told you that I do not think there is any jealousy, properly so called, in the character of Othello... Iago's suggestions... are quite new to him; they do not correspond with any thing of a like nature previously in his mind.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When constructing or judging character action, ensure that emotional responses (e.g., jealousy) either arise from established predisposition or are plausibly instigated by new information. Avoid attributing long‑standing traits to characters who have shown no prior disposition (anti-pattern: retrofitting a vice to explain behavior).

rubrics_metrics.name: Hamlet-type character: thoughtfulness vs practical action
rubrics_metrics.description: ‘Hamlet's character is the prevalence of the abstracting and generalizing habit over the practical... every incident sets him thinking... impelled, at last, by mere accident to effect his object.’
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To depict a Hamlet-like figure, foreground intellectual abstraction, hesitation, and inward reflection that impede practical action; show how accidental circumstance, rather than decisive will, brings about change. Use consistent markers of internality to make such inaction believable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Maxim versus Idea (principle) distinction
rubrics_metrics.description: ‘A Maxim is a conclusion upon observation of matters of fact, and is merely retrospective: an Idea, or ... a Principle, carries knowledge within itself, and is prospective.’ Polonius is cited as a man of maxims.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In characters, essays, or aphoristic writing, distinguish between mere maxims (retrospective sayings) and true ideas/principles that carry explanatory or predictive power. Anti-pattern: a character or writer who only utters maxims will seem limited or one‑eyed (Polonius as a dotard when projecting).

rubrics_metrics.name: Appropriateness of willing counsel versus projecting advice
rubrics_metrics.description: Polonius is admirable while 'descanting on matters of past experience', but 'when he comes to advise or project, he is a mere dotard.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When portraying advisors or when offering guidance in writing, ensure the speaker's authority matches the domain—experience supports retrospective counsel; projecting into future prescriptions requires different credibility. Avoid making characters authoritative beyond their demonstrated competence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dialog authenticity through performance and reserve
rubrics_metrics.description: In the scene with Ophelia: Hamlet begins with 'great and unfeigned tenderness; but, perceiving her reserve and coyness, fancies there are some listeners, and then, to sustain his part, breaks out into all that coarseness.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use shifts in tone and register to reveal a character's self‑monitoring and performance before perceived audiences. Authentic dialogue can show how reserve or the sense of being observed alters speech; use such shifts to convey psychological complexity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition and depiction of love
rubrics_metrics.description: ‘Love is the admiration and cherishing of the amiable qualities of the beloved person, upon the condition of yourself being the object of their action... The qualities of the sexes correspond...’
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When writing love, present it as mutual cherishing of qualities with reciprocal appetite—show admiration, tenderness, constancy, and mutual complementation. Use concrete examples of shared acts and reciprocal valuation rather than abstract sentimental statements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Moral satisfaction in plot resolution
rubrics_metrics.description: On Measure for Measure: 'It is a hateful work... Our feelings of justice are grossly wounded in Angelo's escape. Isabella herself contrives to be unamiable, and Claudio is detestable.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure that plot outcomes and moral reckonings align with the audience's sense of justice or are credibly justified; unresolved or unsatisfying moral consequences can make a work feel offensive or badly conceived. If you subvert moral expectations, provide strong artistic reason or characterization to justify it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish poetic dexterity from genius
rubrics_metrics.description: ‘In the present age it is next to impossible to predict from specimens... that a young man will turn out a great poet... Poetic taste, dexterity in composition, and ingenious imitation, often produce poems that are very promising in appearance. But genius, or the power of doing something new, is another thing.’
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating poetic promise, separate technical skill and imitation from originality (genius). Valuate works not only for craft but for the capacity to innovate; avoid conflating polished imitation with genuine creative potential.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preserve concreteness; avoid abstracting away natural terms
rubrics_metrics.description: ‘Our version of the Bible... has preserved a purity of meaning to many terms of natural objects. Without this holdfast, our vitiated imaginations would refine away language to mere abstractions.’
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Favor concrete, stable terms and images that anchor meaning; resist tendencies toward over-abstraction that strip language of sensory or referential force. In poetic and rhetorical composition, concrete diction sustains imagistic power.

rubrics_metrics.name: Strength of individual imagery versus spatial relation
rubrics_metrics.description: ‘I have the perception of individual images very strong, but a dim one of the relation of place. I remember the man or the tree, but where I saw them I mostly forget.’
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cultivate vivid individual images (characters, objects, gestures), but also attend to spatial and relational context so scenes feel located. Anti-pattern: producing striking images that float detached from setting, which can weaken coherence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Musical delivery and tone variation in recitation
rubrics_metrics.description: Coleridge's recitation of Spenser: 'I particularly bear in mind the sensible diversity of tone and rhythm with which he gave:-- "Sweet Thames! run softly till I end my song," the concluding line of each of the ten strophes.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When composing lyric lines, consider how they will be delivered—varied tone and rhythm enhance effect. Practice reading aloud to shape prosody and to ensure lines carry the intended musical quality in performance.
